chapter.name: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
chapter.blurb: The discovery of cells and microorganisms through the microscope, the structure and shapes of cells, levels of body organisation, the diversity of microorganisms, and their roles in decomposition, nitrogen fixation, fermentation and oxygen production.

scope_in.item: Explain how curved lenses and early microscopes such as Robert Hooke's and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's let people see cells and microorganisms for the first time
Describe the three basic parts common to a cell - the cell membrane, the cytoplasm and the nucleus - and their functions, using the onion peel and cheek cell activities
Describe extra plant-cell structures - the cell wall, plastids such as chloroplasts, and the vacuole - and their functions
Explain that the shape and structure of a cell, such as a muscle cell or a nerve cell, relates to the function it performs
State the levels of organisation of the body - cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism - and describe multicellular organisms
Define microorganisms and classify them as unicellular or multicellular, using examples such as bacteria, Amoeba, fungi and algae observed in pond water and soil suspension
State that microorganisms are found almost everywhere, including inside the human body and in extreme environments, and that viruses are microscopic and acellular
Explain how microorganisms decompose plant and animal waste into manure and produce biogas, and describe Rhizobium's role in fixing nitrogen in legume root nodules
Explain fermentation by yeast in making bread and by Lactobacillus in making curd, idli, dosa and bhatura
Describe microalgae such as Spirulina, their role in producing oxygen and as food, and the basic steps of farming Spirulina
Explain why the cell is the basic unit of life, and describe how a bacterial cell (with a nucleoid instead of a nucleus) differs from plant, animal, fungal, algal and protozoan cells

concepts.name: Discovering the invisible world: microscopes and lenses
concepts.description: How curved lenses and early microscopes, built by Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, first revealed cells and microorganisms too small to see with the naked eye.
concepts.idea: A lens bends light to make small things look bigger, and the microscope revealed a hidden world of living things too small to see with the naked eye.
concepts.rule: A curved piece of glass, thick in the middle and thin at the edges like a lentil seed, was found to make small things look bigger and so was called a lens. Over time lenses were improved and became more powerful, leading from simple magnifying glasses to microscopes. In 1665 Robert Hooke published Micrographia, a book of detailed drawings of tiny things seen through his microscope, which magnified objects 200 to 300 times. He looked at a thin slice of cork and saw many small, empty spaces that reminded him of a honeycomb; he called each space a cell, the first time the word was used in science. Around the same time, in the 1660s, the Dutch scientist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built better lenses and more useful microscopes, and was the first person to clearly see and describe tiny living things such as bacteria and blood cells, which is why he is known as the Father of Microbiology.
concepts.example: A water-filled round-bottom flask acts like a magnifying glass and makes letters on a page look bigger, the same idea behind early lenses and microscopes.

concepts.name: Structure of a cell
concepts.description: The basic parts of a cell seen under a microscope in onion peel and cheek cell samples, and the extra plant-cell structures such as the cell wall, plastids and vacuole.
concepts.idea: A cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus; plant cells also have a rigid cell wall, plastids such as chloroplasts, and usually a large vacuole.
concepts.rule: All living beings are made up of cells. In Activity 2.2, a stained onion peel viewed under a microscope shows closely arranged, nearly rectangular cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm and nucleus. In Activity 2.3, stained human cheek cells appear polygon-shaped and show three main parts: the cell membrane (the outer layer), the nucleus (a round structure in the middle, covered by a thin membrane) and the cytoplasm (the space between them). The cell membrane is porous and controls the entry of materials needed for life and the exit of waste. Cytoplasm contains compounds such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats and mineral salts, and most life processes occur there. The nucleus regulates all the activities and growth of the cell. Plant cells, like onion peel cells, have an extra outer layer called the cell wall, which gives rigidity and strength. Plant cells also contain rod-shaped plastids; some plastids, called chloroplasts, contain chlorophyll, are green, and help in photosynthesis, while plastids in non-green parts help store substances. Plant cells also have a large, empty-looking vacuole that stores substances, removes waste and helps maintain the shape and support of the cell; in animal cells, vacuoles are usually absent or, if present, small.
concepts.example: Onion peel cells viewed under a microscope show a cell wall, cytoplasm and nucleus, while cheek cells show only a cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus.

concepts.name: Cell shape, function and levels of organisation
concepts.description: How a cell's shape suits its job, using muscle cells and nerve cells as examples, and how cells build up into tissues, organs, organ systems and a whole organism.
concepts.idea: The shape of a cell suits its function, and cells are organised into tissues, organs, organ systems and a whole organism.
concepts.rule: Different cells have different shapes and structures that suit the functions they perform. Cheek cells are thin and flat, forming a protective lining on the inner surface of the cheek. Nerve cells (neurons) are long and branched, which helps them reach different parts of the body and pass on messages quickly. A muscle cell is shaped like a spindle, while a nerve cell is long with branches. Plant cells also vary in shape, being rectangular, elongated, oval or tube-like, with some long tubes helping carry water through the plant. In the food pipe, thin, flexible, spindle-shaped muscle cells contract and relax in a wave-like manner to push food to the stomach; in the stomach, muscle cells churn the food while other lining cells produce digestive juices and acid. The body of a living organism is organised from simple to complex: a cell (the basic unit of life, like a brick is the basic unit of a wall) groups into a tissue, tissues organise into an organ, organs work together as an organ system, and all the organ systems together make a complete organism. The life of a complex organism begins with a single cell, the egg, which divides repeatedly to form a many-celled, multicellular organism; animals, including humans, and plants are multicellular. The yolk of an ostrich egg is itself a single cell, the largest known cell, about 130 mm to 170 mm in diameter.

concepts.name: Microorganisms: types and where they live
concepts.description: What microorganisms are, how they are grouped as unicellular or multicellular, and where they are found, based on observing pond water and soil suspension.
concepts.idea: Microorganisms are living things too small to see with the naked eye; they can be single-celled or many-celled and are found almost everywhere, including inside our bodies.
concepts.rule: Some living organisms are made up of just one or very few cells and cannot be seen with the naked eye; these are called microorganisms or microbes (micro means very small, organisms means living beings). Bacteria and Amoeba are unicellular (one cell); some fungi and algae are multicellular (many cells). In Activity 2.4, pond or stagnant water observed under a microscope (which magnifies 100 to 400 times) shows organisms such as Amoeba (Protozoa, single cell, moving, irregular shape) and Paramecium (Protozoa, single cell, moves with specialised structures), as recorded in Table 2.1. In Activity 2.5, a soil suspension is made by mixing soil with water and letting it settle; observed under a microscope it shows organisms such as bread mould and mould (Fungi, branched filaments, no chlorophyll), algae (spherical, with chlorophyll) and bacteria (spherical, comma, spiral or rod-shaped, with hair-like structures), as recorded in Table 2.2. Microorganisms are found everywhere: in water, soil, air, on leaves, stems and roots, inside our bodies (including gut bacteria that help digestion), and even in extreme environments such as hot water springs and snow-cold zones as well as moderate temperatures. Viruses are microscopic and acellular; they multiply only when they enter a living cell and may infect plants, animals or bacteria, sometimes causing disease. Pickles and murabbas usually resist infection because the high concentration of salt or sugar added as preservatives does not allow microorganisms to grow.

concepts.name: Microbes at work: decomposition, nitrogen fixation and fermentation
concepts.description: How microorganisms decompose waste into manure and biogas, how Rhizobium fixes nitrogen for legumes, and how yeast and Lactobacillus ferment bread, idli, dosa and curd.
concepts.idea: Microorganisms decompose waste into manure, produce biogas, fix nitrogen in legume roots, and ferment food such as bread and curd.
concepts.rule: In Activity 2.7, fruit and vegetable peels buried in soil turn, after two to three weeks, into dark-coloured manure that is rich in nutrients; this happens because fungi and bacteria in the soil break down the plant waste into simpler, nutrient-rich substances, a process called decomposition, which needs optimal temperature and moisture. Microorganisms similarly decompose fallen leaves and the bodies of dead animals, returning nutrients to the soil. Some bacteria live without oxygen and decompose plant and animal waste or household wastewater to release biogas, a mixture mainly of carbon dioxide and a high proportion of methane, used as fuel for cooking, heating, generating electricity and running vehicles. Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty (1938-2020) developed, in 1971, a bacterium that could break down oil spills, and his discovery received a patent in 1980, a right given so that no one else can copy, use or sell an invention without permission. Some bacteria, such as Rhizobium, live in swollen root nodules of legumes like beans, peas and lentils, trapping nitrogen from the air and making it useful for the plant, which is why farmers grow legumes in rotation to naturally increase soil nitrogen. In Activity 2.8, yeast (a fungus) added to dough respires and breaks down food to release energy, releasing carbon dioxide that forms bubbles and makes the dough soft and fluffy, and a small amount of alcohol that gives it a different smell; this is used in making bread, cakes and more, and bacteria such as Lactobacillus similarly ferment batter for idli and dosa and dough for bhatura. In Activity 2.9, Lactobacillus in curd feeds on the sugar in milk (lactose), multiplies, and ferments the milk into curd, producing lactic acid, which makes curd sour; these bacteria grow well in warm conditions, so curd forms in a warm bowl but not a cool one.
concepts.example: Rhizobium bacteria live in root nodules of legumes such as peas and beans and trap nitrogen from the air for the plant to use.

concepts.name: Microalgae and the cell as the basic unit of life
concepts.description: Microalgae such as Spirulina and their role in producing oxygen and food, and why the cell is the basic unit of life, including how a bacterial cell differs from other cells.
concepts.idea: Microalgae are tiny plant-like organisms that produce much of Earth's oxygen and are farmed as food, and the cell is the basic unit of life common to every living thing, though bacterial cells lack a true nucleus.
concepts.rule: Microalgae are microscopic plant-like organisms living in water, soil, air and even on trees; they make their own food using sunlight, release oxygen while doing so, and produce more than half of Earth's oxygen supply. They are rich in nutrients and are a food source for many aquatic animals; some, such as Spirulina, Chlorella and Diatoms, are used by humans as health supplements and medicines, and microalgae also help clean water and are used to make biofuel. Pollution, climate change and habitat destruction threaten microalgal diversity, so conserving them protects the environment, oxygen balance, food security and livelihoods; Spirulina, for example, is rich in protein (more than 60 per cent of its body weight) and vitamin B12, and can be farmed in a clear glass tank kept away from direct sunlight, filled with pond water and living Spirulina, stirred twice a week, and harvested after three to six weeks by filtering through a fine cloth. The body of all living organisms is made up of cells: multicellular organisms have many cells that specialise and cooperate, while unicellular organisms such as bacteria and protozoa carry out all their functions in a single cell; other microbes, like algae and fungi, can be either, for example yeast is a unicellular fungus while mould is a multicellular fungus. Like plant and animal cells, microbial cells are surrounded by a cell membrane; fungal cells additionally have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesise; bacteria lack a well-defined nucleus and nuclear membrane, having instead a nucleoid, which distinguishes them from the cells of yeast, protozoa, algae, fungi, plants and animals. An electron microscope magnifies a cell about 10,00,000 times, revealing more structures than a light microscope can show.
concepts.example: Spirulina is a microalga that can be farmed in a tank and harvested after three to six weeks as a protein-rich superfood.

questions.q: Explain why the chapter concludes that a cell is the basic unit of life, using both unicellular and multicellular organisms as examples.
questions.a: In unicellular organisms such as bacteria and protozoa, a single cell carries out every function needed for survival; in multicellular organisms such as plants and animals, many specialised cells cooperate to keep the organism alive; because every living organism, whether made of one cell or many, is built from and depends on cells, the cell is considered the basic unit of life.

questions.q: Do you think farming microalgae like Spirulina is a good way to address both nutrition and livelihood needs? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Yes, because Spirulina is rich in protein and vitamin B12 and can be grown in a simple tank and harvested in a few weeks, so it can provide affordable nutrition while also becoming a feasible source of income for growers.

questions.q: Create a short awareness message, in your own words, explaining to your community why microalgae should be conserved and how they help us.
questions.a: A message explaining that microalgae make more than half of Earth's oxygen, feed aquatic animals, and can be farmed as food and medicine, but pollution, climate change and habitat loss threaten them, so conserving water bodies and reducing pollution helps protect microalgae and the oxygen balance and food security they support.
